To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) white men are more likely than women or people of color to have white male contacts, (2) the networks of white men are comprised of more high status contacts than the networks of women or people of minority racial/ethnic groups, (3) white men receive more job leads than women or people in minority racial/ethnic categories, and (4) gender homophilous connections offer greater job finding help than do other types of contacts.
white men have more and higher status contacts in their networks, and these contacts provide them with more information about job opportunities.
people in white men’s networks receive more job leads, have higher status connections, and have greater access to job finding assistance than people in other networks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which gender and race intersect to shape access to social capital.
how social networks are structured by race, gender, and class and how these social structures affect social capital accumulation and job finding assistance.
the ways in which gender and race are embedded in the structure of social networks and the consequences that this has for social capital.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
gender and racial homophily in networks is associated with the receipt of more social capital.
the "old boys' network" is a real phenomenon and that it is a powerful source of social capital.
gendered and racial networks do not provide the same level of social capital.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
white males have access to more social capital than women and minorities, but that gender homophily is a key determinant of social capital in the job finding process.
the gender and race of the network matters, and that the benefits of social capital accrue to everyone, not just white males.
white men benefit from a double advantage in the labor market.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the gendered and racial composition of networks matter for social capital returns.
social capital is not a neutral resource that can be accessed equally by all.
gendered networks are not only a source of inequality but also a mechanism through which inequality is reproduced.
